passages.text: A qualitative exploration of dentists' opioid prescribing decisions within U.S. veterans affairs facilities
Supplemental Digital Content is Available in the Text.
Qualitative interviews with dentists offered possible intervention targets to expand implementation of safe opioid prescribing for acute dental pain management within the Veterans Affairs.
Abstract

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is the largest integrated healthcare system in the United States and provides dental care to approximately one-half million veterans annually. In response to the opioid crisis, the VA released several opioid risk mitigation strategies. Although opioid prescribing by VA dentists has decreased on the whole, the implementation experiences at the level of dentists remains unclear. Our objective was to explore the barriers and facilitators that affect opioid decision making for management of acute dental pain among VA dentists. Dentists practicing in the VA facilities with the highest and lowest volume of opioid prescriptions were recruited. Standardized qualitative interviews by telephone followed a semistructured guide designed around the Capability (C), Opportunity (O), Motivation (M), and Behaviour (B) model. Audio recordings were transcribed and independently double-coded using NVivo to identify potential targets for future guideline-based opioid interventions. Of 395 eligible general and specialty dentists, 90 (24.8%) completed an interview representing 33 VA facilities. Opportunities for prescribing opioids included 1) completion of dental procedures associated with acute dental pain, 2) caring for patients who presented with existing dental pain, and 3) responding to patient opioid requests. Capabilities included using resources (eg, electronic medical records), clinical judgement (eg, evaluation of medical history including medication use), communication skills, and ability to screen for opioid misuse. Motivation themes focused on alleviating patients' acute dental pain. Barriers and facilitators of opioid prescribing varied across facilities. The results can offer intervention targets for continued opioid risk mitigation efforts.
1. Background

Pharmacologic management of acute dental pain includes the use of opioid and nonopioid analgesics. Safe and effective use of these medications requires consideration of specific patient and clinical factors combined with clinical judgement. Despite recommendations and evidence supporting the efficacy of nonopioids such as acetaminophen (APAP) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen to manage acute pain, these options have been “historically underappreciated by many dentists,” thereby contributing to opioid over prescribing by dentists practicing in the United States.

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) provides the greatest volume of dental care in the U.S. caring for approximately one-half million veterans in 2020. Managing acute dental pain among the veteran population can be uniquely challenging for several reasons. First, up to 50% of veteran's experience chronic pain—a portion of which involve management with opioids. Perhaps related, many veterans have histories of substance use disorders and other mental health challenges that may affect safe options for managing acute dental pain.

In addition to federal and state efforts, the VA implemented system-wide efforts to decrease opioid prescribing. In 2012, almost 25% of veterans had filled a prescription for an opioid in a VA outpatient pharmacy. By 2016, this number decreased by approximately a quarter. However, similar to the national landscape, assessing the implementation of VA opioid mitigation efforts focused largely on measuring changes in opioid prescribing rates. Although such data are important, they offer no insights into the mechanisms or pathways that contributed to the modified patterns of opioid prescribing at the dentist level. Existing barriers that adversely affect opioid prescribing decisions as well as facilitators of safe prescribing remain unclear. By using qualitative research methods, this study offers a complementary approach to inform future implementation of opioid risk mitigation efforts within the VA. The aim of this study was to describe the barriers and facilitators that affected opioid decision making for management of acute dental pain as reported by a national sample of VA dentists.
2. Methods

This study used qualitative research methods and a theoretically informed approach, the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF). Theoretical domains framework specified behavioral determinants or domains that influenced human behavior. Each domain mapped to a larger construct within the Capability (C), Opportunity (O), Motivation (M), and Behaviour (B) (COM-B) model which served as the conceptual model of implementation as outlined by Atkins et al. The targeted behavior for exploration was VA dentists' opioid prescribing. The COM-B model hypothesized that a dentist's capabilities to prescribe opioids consistent with evidence (ie, knowledge), opportunities, (ie, caring for patients who request opioids), and motivation (ie, alleviating pain) influenced their opioid prescribing decisions. Factors within each of the 3 constructs were subsequently identified as a barrier or facilitator to prescribing opioids consistent with evidence.
2.1. Development of interview guide

An initial draft of semistructured questions was generated using deductive and inductive approaches with input from a primary care physician, 2 clinical pharmacists, 2 doctorate-level public health experts, and several VA dentists who had opioid-related expertise. Questions targeted the behavioral domains within the TDF and were iteratively refined based on feedback from the expert team and results of cognitive testing with 2 VA dentists. A third VA dentist reviewed the guide for comprehension, clarity, and face validity. The final interview guide, shown in Supplement materials (available at http://links.lww.com/PAIN/B698), was used for all subsequent interviews.
2.2. Ethical oversight

Research activities had full approval from the Edward Hines, Jr VA Hospital Institutional Review Board (protocol #17-051). The data set supporting the conclusions of this article is not available because of the consents obtained from participants.
2.3. Sampling strategy

Using the VAMC Corporate Data Warehouse, facility-level rates of opioid prescribing between 2015 and 2017 were calculated. The 5 highest and lowest opioid prescribing facilities within each of the 4 U.S. Census Regions were identified. Within those 40 facilities, dentists with active VA appointments who had at least 1 opioid prescription filled in 2016 to 2017 were eligible. An a priori sample size of 96 was set for grant budgetary purposes to be modified based on reaching data saturation. Variability was maximized by balancing recruitment across national regions in the United States.
2.4. Dentist recruitment and data collection

Before recruitment initiation, respective chiefs of dentistry received an e-mail from the Director of the Oral Health Quality Group within the VA Office of Dentistry introducing the research and a second e-mail in support from the Assistant Under Secretary for Health for Dentistry. Recruitment materials made no mention of opioid prescribing rates within any facility. Eligible dentists were subsequently emailed in waves with an informational opt-out letter. Three experienced female VA employed research coordinators (P.S., M.P.H.; A.V., M.P.H.; I.K., M.P.H.) with training and experience in qualitative interviewing attempted to contact dentists using e-mail, telephone, and Skype messaging—the primary VA communication platform at the time. A maximum of 3 attempts with each approach was attempted. All communication described that this study was aimed at understanding dentists' decisions around pain management. Dentists willing to participate were scheduled for an interview and research assistants contacted them using Skype with audio only. Both interviewers and dentists were alone in a private space during the interviews. All study procedures were explained, and audio-recorded verbal consent was required with optional audio recording of the interview. Field notes were maintained separately. A qualitative expert (L.K.S.) provided feedback on the first 3 interviews and met weekly with interviewers. Per VA guidelines, dentists received no reimbursement. Audio-recorded interviews were subsequently transcribed verbatim.
2.5. Data analyses

Anonymized transcripts were uploaded into NVivo software for data management and coding. A behavioral scientist with qualitative expertise (L.K.S.) and experience using the TDF led the coding and interpretation of data working with 2 experienced coders (P.S., M.P.H.; T.B., M.P.H.). Both received training in the TDF framework and COM-B model. Coding and interpretation of the data were conducted consistent with thematic content analyses. Three coders (L.K.S., P.S., T.B.) independently read 10 transcripts several times before meeting. Using deductive methods, an initial draft of the codebook was developed based on relevant COM-B domains. Through discussions, the 3 coders identified specific text in 5 transcripts that aligned with each coded domain while clarifying definitions and expanding the codebook. Once complete, the remaining 5 transcripts were independently coded and the 3 met to discuss results. Comparison of results suggested a strong shared understanding of the codes. Two coders (P.S. and T.B.) independently coded the remaining transcripts with a resulting kappa of 0.92. Discrepancies were discussed, and consensus was achieved. Facilitated by NVivo, text for each code across all transcripts was reviewed and synthesized through additional discussion involving all coders. These results were then mapped onto the domains of capability, opportunity, or motivation and further categorized as barriers and facilitators. Feedback on findings was obtained from 2 dentists on the team and the interviewers.
3. Results

Recruitment was initiated on September 24, 2019, and data collection ended on July 29, 2020. The CONSORT diagram is shown in Figure 1; in brief, of 314 eligible dentists working in 40 different VA facilities, 90 (28.7%) completed an interview representing 33 different VA facilities. As presented in Table 1, participants were predominantly White (65.9%), male (57.8%), general dentists (80%) and had practiced an average of 20 years (range 9-30 years). One dentist, a VA Chief, did not have an active license to prescribe opioids at the time of interview; however, they met all inclusion criteria. Two dentists refused audio recording, so detailed notes were taken. Interviews ranged in length from 11 to 50 minutes averaging 35 minutes.

3.1. Opioid prescribing over time and reasons for changing

Recognizing that most respondents had graduated from dental training before the emergence of the opioid epidemic, the interview began by asking dentists to describe how, if any, their personal prescribing of opioids may have changed since completing dental training and why. Most, including graduates as recent as 2015, expressed that they had decreased the use of opioids. Consistent with the guidelines, the most common changes were reported to be decreasing from 7 days of opioids to 5 days or from 5 days to 3 days. Two oral surgeons reported more significant changes from “routinely prescribing 14 days” and the other reporting “30 days of opioids following oral surgery” down to “a few days if at all.”

“-the level of caution has changed in prescribing opiates because of opioid dependence and the risk of opioid addiction. So, when I was a young dentist, I mean, it was not abnormal for me to give 2 weeks of opioid medication for post extraction comfort, but now I'm very careful of what types of extractions I prescribe opioids with and how much I prescribe opiates … I always review the file to determine whether the patient has a history of opioid dependence or if they're on any other opiates at the time that I give them a new prescription.” GD-04-71

Over half of the sample attributed their decreased opioid use to increased knowledge of the addictive potential of opioids and recognizing that opioids were over prescribed for pain management. Many highlighted the effectiveness of NSAIDS and APAP to manage pain. The increased knowledge was attributed to continuing education and professional journals along with the national media reporting on the opioid crisis. Access to opioid histories through VAMC medical records or the state PDMP was also important. As expressed by 1 general dentist:

“I think as you practice longer, you become more comfortable telling patients that they really don't need an opioid or explain to them why they don't. You don't get bullied by patients quite as much as you practice longer.” GD-03-98

For 1 dentist, the turning point was having a family member became addicted to opioids. Gaining experience as a dentist was important to a few who decreased opioid prescribing as they became more proficient at dental procedures or honed their communication skills related to pain management. As expressed by 1 dentist:
“The dosage I prescribed is fairly small, so I'm not too concerned about the risks of the opioid medication itself as they're taking it.” SP-04-79

Conversely, 14 dentists perceived that they had always been low opioid prescribers because of (1) completing dental training when opioid awareness was high, (2) conducting fewer painful procedures, and (3) caring for a population with substance abuse histories. Although not common, perceiving oneself to be a low prescriber could be associated with a diminished concern about opioid risks as reflected by this specialty dentist:
3.2. Capability and opportunity: determine clinical need for an opioid and apply clinical judgement

Dentists described 3 common situations (opportunities) where opioid prescribing decisions were required: following dental procedures or surgeries, evaluating patients who presented with existing acute dental complaints, and responding to patient requests for opioids. In all situations, clinical judgement, a specific group of capabilities, informed the decisions. Clinical judgement, based on the thematic analysis, involved 3 domains of knowledge: (1) procedural considerations, (2) the patient's medical history including current medications, and (3) assessment of the current or expected pain intensity.
3.3. Capability: procedural considerations

Two distinct approaches to determining whether a dental procedure required opioids to manage the pain were apparent in the interviews. One approach involved identifying specific procedures or surgeries that might require an opioid, if not otherwise contraindicated. These determinations were often based on past experiences treating patients. However, there was poor agreement. Specifically, some dentists considered opioids for “surgical tooth extractions,” “root canals,” or “acute pulpitis,” while others believed that opioids were typically not needed for those situations. This procedure-based approach was contrasted with dentists who considered the level of invasiveness and complexity of the procedure or surgery when determining if an opioid was required. These dentists described focusing on the degree of tissue or bone trauma and less on the procedure itself.
3.4. Capability: evaluate patients' medical history and medications for contraindications

“The highest risk is mixed medications… so many times the psychotropic medications they take, could interact with the opioids and lead to more sedation or respiratory depression. So, that's always a concerning factor for all of us here.” GD-02-47

Unlike community dentists, all dentists within the VA had access to patients' medical records. Furthermore, all reported that they used VA electronic medical records (EMR) in making decisions about opioid prescribing. Medical histories were evaluated for substance use, chronic pain, current medications, and comorbidities. For many, having access to patients' substance use histories and chronic pain treatment were fundamental to their opioid decisions. Most indicated that opioids would not be considered for patients with a history of substance abuse or for those currently on opioids for chronic pain. In addition, knowledge of patients' current medications was important to evaluate for possible interactions with pain medications. Many respondents highlighted the issue of benzodiazepines and other psychotropics interacting with opioids as shown in this quote:

Additional concerns focused on NSAIDs interacting with some anticoagulants and allergies to NSAIDs, APAP, or opioids. Finally, patients' general health status and the presence of medical comorbidities were often mentioned as a factor influencing the use of opioids. Specifically, diabetes, liver or kidney problems, and gastrointestinal problems were identified as factors that affected pain management choices. Less frequently mentioned patient factors included age of the patient, weight, and fall risk.
3.5. Capability: assess current or expected pain intensity
“The procedures that I do. I've been doing it long enough that I know what's going to hurt quite a bit and what's not and kind of the patient-what you pick up on their pain tolerance.” GD-02-56

Approximately half of the dentists attempted to assess or anticipate the pain intensity that patients might be experiencing. Opioids were often considered when moderate to severe pain intensity was expected. Several dentists mentioned that they attempted to factor in individual differences in pain thresholds. Assessing pain intensity for many dentists approximated an educated guess more than a formal assessment using validated measures. In advance of dental procedures, only a few asked patients to describe how they had managed pain in the past. Dentists' confidence in their ability to accurately assess patients' pain varied. For example, a more confident dentist stated:

“Like I said, I think the patient's pain tolerance. I think if they are an extremely intolerant patient, I might just give a small amount. I try not to be influenced by people that bring it up (needing an opioid) and start begging and that kind of thing because I get suspicious of whether they are wanting it strictly for the procedure I completed or for some other reason. So, I try not to let myself be influenced by them.” GD-01-53
This was contrasted with a less confident dentist.
3.6. Motivation: alleviate pain and prescribing opioids “just in case”

In virtually all cases of opioid prescribing, the dentists' primary motivation was to alleviate dental pain and the prescription was offered assuming it would be needed. However, 3 dentists' described situations where an opioid was prescribed in case it was needed. These included: working in a rural setting where “patients sometimes lived 200 miles away” and returning to clinic was challenging, delays in care because of dental specialist referrals, and seeing patients “on a Friday when communicating over the weekend might be difficult.” In all 3 examples, the dentists expressed that they wanted to make sure the patients' pain was managed.
3.7. Opportunity: frequency of patient requests for opioids

Dentists reported that patient opioid requests were common. Only 2 reported that no one they had treated in the past year had asked for an opioid. The frequency of opioid requests varied widely from “a couple times a year” or “once every 2 months” to “probably at least 90% of the time.” Some dentists linked requests to procedures like “one out of every 5 extractions.” Although variation in frequency of opioid requests was evident within both the general and specialist dentists, oral surgeons and dentists working in emergency triage or emergency departments tended to report the most frequent requests. General dentists noted that “walk in” patients frequently requested opioids. A few dentists believed that patient requests for opioids had diminished in the past few years with some patients actively seeking nonopioid options for pain relief.
3.8. Capabilities: manage patient requests for opioids

The interviews provided insight into how dentists responded to opioid requests, particularly when an opioid was not indicated. The first step involved interpreting the patients' motivation for wanting an opioid. Dentists perceived motivations to range from patients with dental-related anxiety or fear of pain but not “opioid seeking” to patients seeking opioids for abuse or dependence. Three different responses to patient requests for opioids were used: (1) refusing to prescribe opioids with an explanation or education on nonopioid options; (2) refusing to prescribe opioids with direct expression of concern that the patient may be abusing opioids, with or without a providing a referral; and (3) consulting with the patient's primary care provider or pain specialist before deciding on whether or not to prescribe.

“I mean I don't try to debate with them; I just refuse to prescribe them (opioids). I tell them it's not indicated and why and that's it. You know, I don't hedge, and I don't hesitate. I just tell them straight out." SP-01-34

“I try to educate the patient. I try to focus on the evidence that Tylenol-ibuprofen combination is more effective on dental pain than an opioid and I try to talk about getting to the root cause. I'm a little bit more nervous when it comes to those patients because you never know that they're not an addict when it comes to pain medication. That's a little bit harder of a situation to diffuse than an antibiotic.” GD-04-78

Approximately one half of the dentists reported that they typically refused to prescribe the opioid explaining it was not needed. Among those, many provided education on the efficacy of NSAIDs and APAP for pain control along with the risk of opioid dependence. However, as shown in these quotes, dentists varied in their comfort with managing some of these requests:

“I don't - like - provide counselling for patients but I don't have any problem being clear with patients that based on their prescribing history, which I can see on the computer, that I'm not comfortable prescribing additional opioids or I'm concerned about the amount they are already being prescribed.” GD-03-58

In refusing to prescribe, some dentists informed patients that they had evidence from medical records or other sources that they had an existing or recent opioid prescription. Having such documentation seemed to increase some dentists' level of comfort communicating with patients about their opioid abuse concerns. For example:

“A lot of times, I will go back to the patient after I have checked the database and I will try to confront them and usually say, well, you've been given a lot of narcotics previously and I try to give them something non-narcotic based, usually an anti-inflammatory. Sometimes I'm successful and sometimes I'm not. If they're still sensitive to that or still want a narcotic, I'll further reduce it to only 2 days.” GD-03-38

However, 3 dentists expressed that depending on the situation, they might prescribe opioids in response to a patient request even if they did not feel they were indicated, justifying that they would “limit the amount” to 2 or 3 days. As reflected in this quote:

“Usually, in dental, here at the VA where I work, we don't prescribe any narcotics from here. If the patient is requesting it or he gets upset, we always refer them to their primary care doctor. They are the ones running the programs and the contract for pain management.” GD-03-05

Approximately one third of the dentists described managing patients' opioid requests by involving other healthcare providers or specialists. Among those dentists, some seemed to defer all opioid prescribing to the primary care provider, not just opioid requests from veterans, suggesting this was a VA site-specific approach to avoid multiple prescribers as shown in this quote:

“I usually let them know that it's a joint decision between me and their primary care provider. So, before I would just hand over a prescription, I would indicate that I need to discuss this with their medical provider as well to determine if this is the most appropriate medication for them.” GD-02-47
Other dentists preferred to discuss the necessity of opioids for acute pain with the primary care provider before deciding how to respond to an opioid request as reflected here:
3.9. Capabilities: managing acute pain in veterans on opioids for chronic pain

“Our chronic pain management patients who are already on high levels, and so, I wouldn't prescribe any more. If I were going to, I would have to talk to their chronic pain doctor with them to proceed with caution.” GD-04-16
Management of acute dental pain in veterans on long-term opioids for chronic pain routinely involved consultation with a physician. As reflected in this response:

“Typically, on our screen, we see opioid contract and we read that and we try to stay within the guidelines of that; if it's a certain amount they cannot exceed, if it's necessary, we call the physician and we talk to them and say, hey I just had to do a surgical extraction, it was really difficult and this guy is going to be in pain for the next 4 to 5 days. What do you think?” (SP-04-67-051920)

Many dentists explained that they identified veterans on long-term opioid therapy by a written pain agreement or “opioid contract,” as dentists referred to them, which was prominent in the medical record. These written agreements were initiated between the patient and the prescribing provider of the long-term opioids who was most often identified as the patients' primary care physician. Most commonly, if the dentist believed that additional opioids were needed for the acute dental pain, they reportedly contacted the provider designated in the pain agreement as reflected in the following quote:

“So a lot of times if they're being seen for chronic pain and those are being prescribed in that regard I'll also say like, you know you're being-it's being prescribed by Dr. So and So from the pain clinic and that should hold you for the procedure. There's no reason to have extra.” (SP-01-13).
However, several dentists expressed a belief that long-term opioid use offered sufficient pain relief for most of the acute dental pain patients experienced.
3.10. Capabilities: use resources to support pain management decisions

Knowledge was fundamental in making decisions about pain management and opioids. Numerous dentists mentioned using the VA guidelines and published information as a resource that informed their pain management decisions. Similar resources less commonly mentioned were material published by the American Dental Association, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, American Medical Association, and other professional dental organizations. A few dentists reported taking online educational courses on pain management and opioids typically required to maintain their license. Many dentists attributed these resources to their knowledge of NSAIDS and APAP as a first-line approach to pain management.
Although access varied by facility, when available, pain management, psychology, social work, substance abuse, or neurology were resources that supported evidence-based prescribing.

Additional resources focused on providing patient-level information that factored into clinical judgement and aided in determining safe options for pain management. The EMR was used to obtain information on patients' medical comorbidities, psychiatric histories including substance use disorders, current medications including opioids, and allergies that were viewed as critical to identifying contraindications for pain medication decisions.

“The VA has a separate system other than the state PDMP. So they have this STORM system that is used more frequently. When I'm seeing VA patients-it's used as a tool to predict potential opioid abuse by -by a particular patient within the VA system. And so I guess I use that on a fairly regular basis the VA. So using the state PDMP for the VA patients, you know, is frankly not that necessary.” SP-04-79-070820

In addition to reviewing medical records for opioid agreements to identify chronic pain patients on opioids, some dentists checked patients' prior receipt of opioid prescriptions using the VA Stratification Tool for Opioid Risk Management (VA STORM) or the state-level prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP). Veterans affairs STORM is a web-based tool developed within the VA to assist in clinical decision making on opioids. STORM uses patient-level information and predictive modeling to estimate a risk score for serious adverse opioid-related events. Prescription drug monitoring programs are state-level electronic databases that track patient-level information on controlled substance prescription fills (ie, opioids and benzodiazepines). As described by 1 dentist,

“I think it's because there are more things in place to check what patients are getting and before there was no way of knowing what patients were getting and I would typically give 5 days worth of pain medication which I don't do any longer.” GD-02-93

State mandates for PDMP registration and use vary with only some requiring registration to maintain a dental license. Most respondents reported having registered with their state PDMP, although some were uncertain of their registration status. Unlike community dentists, practitioners within VA are not required to maintain an active state dental licensure where they practice. As a result, a few dentists reported difficulty registering with the PDMP because they were licensed outside the state in which they practiced. Registration did not equate to PDMP utilization with some acknowledging that they never or rarely used the PDMP. Interestingly, a few dentists expressed that VA employees were required to follow the federal guidelines so that state PDMP mandates were typically not relevant to them. Others expressed that they only prescribed within the VA, so they did not need to be registered with the state. Despite the fact that interviews suggested that enforcement of VA opioid guidelines, STORM, or PDMPs was largely voluntary, the use of the resources reportedly decreased opioid prescribing patterns for some dentists. As expressed by one:

“... well, [name of state PDMP] will give me reports over the quarter and they'll describe kind of a profile on your prescriptions related to other dentists within your scope of practice. So, they'll say your prescribing equal to or less than more than most providers.” GD-02-48-041020

Implementation of the CDC opioid prescribing guidelines, which are supported by VA and the American Dental Association, relied largely on self-monitoring. Only a few dentists reported even receiving feedback on their opioid prescribing practices. The exception was one dentist who reported receiving feedback on their individual opioid prescribing from a VA chief. Another received a written report from the state PDMP for self-inspection as described:
Several dentists commented that they were able to review their prescribing histories on their own; however, it was not clear if they had.
3.11. Barriers and facilitators to opioid prescribing along with intervention targets

As presented in Table 2, the results were organized into barriers and facilitators of guideline-based opioid prescribing. Some barriers involved a set of capabilities needed to manage patient requests for opioids such as evaluating pain intensity, screening for opioid abuse, and communication skills. Communication skills involved being able to definitively say no to opioid requests even when the patient protested. Two additional barriers related to dentists not receiving any feedback on their personal opioid prescribing and no enforcement of existing efforts in opioid mitigation.
Barriers and facilitators of Centers for Disease Control guideline-based opioid prescribing for acute dental pain.

Facilitators included knowledge of the recommendations for use of NSAIDs and APAP as well as the risks of opioids. Important resources specific to the VA included the computerized patient record system which is the VA's EMR, STORM, and access, in some facilities, to specialized referrals or pathways for managing patients. Two resources, PDMP access, and licensing requirements for education in opioids and pain management were not VA specific, but noted as facilitators.
4. Discussion

The Department of Veterans Affairs has directed significant effort towards opioid mitigation over the past decade. To date, evaluation of those efforts has relied on reporting quantitative changes in opioid prescribing rates, in coprescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines, and in opioid daily dosages in excess of 100 morphine milligram equivalents at the system level. Less attention has focused on the individual VA dentist level. Using qualitative methods, this study identified several barriers and facilitators of opioid prescribing for acute dental pain.

The results suggested that some dentists lacked communication skills and confidence to assess pain intensity, screen for opioid misuse, and decline some patient requests for opioids. The subjective and multidimensional nature of pain complicates pain assessment. Some dentists, general and specialty, focused on identifying an objective source of pain such as bone or tissue trauma. Although this approach may seem to be objective and may provide reassurance around opioid decisions, the degree of oral trauma is not always correlated with reported pain intensity. In the absence of objective evidence, denying patient opioid requests and expressing concerns related to potential opioid abuse are uncomfortable conversations for many healthcare providers. Approaching patients with abuse concerns can feel confrontational and complicated by the subjective nature of pain. Having access to opioid prescribing histories offered reassurance for some, but not all dentists.

Despite the availability of opioid communication tools on both VA Pain Management (Opioid Safety—Clinical Tools—VHA Pain Management (va.gov)) web site and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention web site, some providers struggled with communication. Mastering communication skills often requires active participation using role playing, modeling, and practice addressing specific scenarios. To address these barriers, future efforts to address opioid mitigation could include one-on-one or group training in communication skills building related to assessment of opioid misuse, concerns about possible misuse, and management of patient requests for opioids.

Additional barriers involved dentists' lack of awareness of their opioid prescribing combined with weak enforcement of existing guidelines or mandates. Audit and feedback is a widely used, effective approach to modifying provider behaviors when there is a goal for comparison. The utility of this approach would likely be greatest in targeting coprescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines or daily dosages of opioids that exceed 50 morphine milligram equivalent where the goal is close to zero prescriptions. Attempting to decrease the number of opioid prescriptions with audit and feedback could be more challenging because the goal for number of opioid prescriptions is unclear. Nonetheless, providing individual feedback and deidentified prescribing rates for dentists with similar practices may be effective for the highest prescribing dentists.

Despite state-level and VA system-wide mandates to use PDMPs, approximately half of the dentists surveyed were not doing so. Less than optimal uptake of PDMP utilization has been reported elsewhere within the VA system. Unlike dentists practicing outside the VA, those within the VA had access to comprehensive EMRs which may have contributed to lower PDMP use. However, a portion of veterans receive opioids from both VA and outside VA. Receipt of opioids outside the VA may not be documented in the VA medical records.

Facilitators that seemed to support dentists' safe prescribing of opioids focused on knowledge, educational requirements, and resources. Considering the VA efforts towards opioid mitigation and U.S. media around the opioid epidemic, it was not surprising that most dentists self-reported that their use of opioids had decreased since graduating from dental training. The accuracy of these reports is uncertain, and decreases in prescribing rates does not equate with CDC guideline-based prescribing.4 Knowledge of the efficacy of NSAIDs and APAP to manage pain, contraindications for opioids, and guidelines limiting the days of opioid coverage were verbalized widely among the sample. Veterans affairs efforts to educate dentists on the current opioid guidelines seem to have been largely successful, at least among the participants. Augmenting VA efforts to provide opioid education, as of 2019, 25 states required continuing education on dental pain management and opioid prescribing to maintain dental licensure.

The VA is an integrated healthcare system allowing dentists to access patients' medical records and their medical providers. This access factored into virtually all dentists' opioid prescribing decisions. Specifically, veterans on long-term opioids prescribed within the VA system could be easily identified through medical records. Furthermore, many facilities had centralized pain management in primary care services with few mentioning the availability of specialized pain management programs or substance abuse specialists. In particular, dentists relied heavily on primary care providers to assist with or manage opioid prescribing decisions for patients on long-term opioids. However, a few dentists also referred opioid-seeking patients who were not on long-term opioids back to their primary care. This likely allowed dentists to avoid uncomfortable conversations with patients but may have placed a burden on other providers. As such, it would be important to understand the impact of centralizing opioid prescribing through primary care on those providers and ensure it is working effectively. Such approaches could strain relations with primary care providers if they are already overwhelmed with numerous patient-related demands.
5. Limitations

As with all qualitative research, despite the large national sample, the extent to which these results generalize is uncertain. Several limitations should be considered. Although the sampling strategy attempted to identify facilities with the highest and lowest opioid prescribing rates, recruitment began in 2019 and prescribing rates were based on data from 2015 to 2017. Furthermore, higher relative rates of opioid prescribing within an institution do not equate to less appropriate use of opioids. No individual-level prescribing data were available; therefore, the dentists who participated may not have been representative of the facility for opioid prescribing. Finally, the sample may have been biased towards dentists with greater interest in pain management and with greater awareness of the opioid epidemic.

Despite limitations, this is the first study to use qualitative methods to explore individual-level opioid decision making among any VA healthcare providers. Strengths of this study include sampling of dentists in VAs across the United States which required numerous interviews to maximize variation in perspectives and reach data saturation. The inquiry was designed using behavior change principles within the COM-B model, and as such, the results may inform future interventions to extend the implementation of existing VA efforts.

In conclusion, this study offered an informal assessment of existing opioid mitigation efforts within VA as expressed in dentists own voices. The results offer possible intervention targets to expand implementation of safe opioid prescribing for acute dental pain management within the VA.
